claims.evidence: NHS: aciclovir is used to treat infections such as cold sores, shingles, chickenpox, genital herpes and herpes simplex eye infections.
claims.newSentence: Aciclovir is an antiviral medicine used for infections such as cold sores, shingles, chickenpox and genital herpes.

claims.evidence: NHS common questions: No medicine or treatment will remove the herpes virus from your body completely.
claims.newSentence: The NHS says no medicine or treatment removes the herpes virus from the body completely.

claims.evidence: NHS lists cold sores, shingles, chickenpox, genital herpes, herpes simplex eye infections; sometimes used to prevent these in people with weakened immune systems.
claims.newSentence: usedFor list

claims.evidence: NHS common questions: stops the herpes virus growing and spreading; controls the infection and helps the immune system deal with it.
claims.newSentence: The NHS says aciclovir stops the herpes virus growing and spreading, which helps the immune system deal with the infection.

claims.evidence: MedlinePlus acyclovir injection/ophthalmic/topical pages: class of antivirals called synthetic nucleoside analogues; works by stopping the spread of the herpes virus in the body. (First-pass mechanism claim confirmed; oral page a681045 not itself seen with this wording.)
claims.newSentence: MedlinePlus describes aciclovir as a synthetic nucleoside analogue antiviral that works by stopping the spread of the herpes virus in the body.

claims.evidence: NHS: you should start to feel better after taking or using aciclovir for a few days; start as soon as you get the first signs of infection.
claims.newSentence: The NHS says people should start to feel better after taking or using aciclovir for a few days, and advises starting as soon as the first signs of infection appear.

claims.evidence: NHS side effects page lists these as common (usually mild).
claims.newSentence: The NHS lists headache, dizziness or feeling faint, feeling or being sick, diarrhoea, stomach ache, rash, itching, tiredness, a high temperature and a skin reaction after exposure to light as common side effects, which are usually mild.

claims.evidence: NHS: Creams are less likely to cause side effects. Some people get mild burning or stinging after using them, but it usually goes away quickly.
claims.newSentence: The NHS says creams are less likely to cause side effects, though some people get mild burning or stinging that usually goes away quickly.

claims.evidence: NHS: If side effects bother you or don't go away, speak to a pharmacist or doctor.
claims.newSentence: For a side effect that bothers someone or does not go away, the NHS suggests speaking to a pharmacist or doctor.

claims.evidence: First pass: NHS advises staying out of bright sun and avoiding sun lamps and sun beds. Retrieved text only lists 'a skin reaction after exposure to light' as a side effect; no avoidance advice was retrieved.
First pass: dizziness advice not to drive, cycle or use machinery. Not in retrieved aciclovir text.
NHS: serious allergic reaction, call 999 (lips, mouth, throat or tongue suddenly swelling, struggling to breathe).
claims.newSentence: A serious allergic reaction, with signs such as sudden swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue or struggling to breathe, needs a 999 call, according to the NHS.

claims.evidence: First pass called allergic reaction and liver/kidney/blood effects 'rare'. Retrieved NHS text lists them as serious effects but the word 'rare' was not in the retrieved text.
NHS: other serious side effects (liver problems, kidney problems, blood cell changes) - call 111.
claims.newSentence: Liver problems, kidney problems and changes to blood cells are also listed as serious side effects; the NHS advises calling NHS 111 if someone using or recently using aciclovir thinks they may be having these.

claims.evidence: NHS aciclovir page: isn't suitable for everyone; tell your doctor if you have kidney problems, are over 65, pregnant or trying to get pregnant, or breastfeeding.
claims.newSentence: The NHS advises telling a doctor before use about kidney problems, being over 65, being pregnant or trying to get pregnant, or breastfeeding.

claims.evidence: First pass: 'NHS says aciclovir can usually be used in pregnancy'. Retrieved NHS text only asks to tell the doctor; reassurance came from a Tayside leaflet and cannot be attributed to the NHS page.
First pass: cream/ointment usually fine in breastfeeding if baby does not touch treated areas; tell doctor before tablets. Not in retrieved text.
emc SmPC: hypersensitivity to aciclovir or valaciclovir is a contraindication.
claims.newSentence: UK product information lists allergy to aciclovir or valaciclovir as a reason the medicine is not used.

claims.evidence: emc leaflets/SmPC: dose may be adjusted for children, people over 65 and kidney problems; elderly renal impairment must be considered.
claims.newSentence: UK patient leaflets say the doctor may adjust treatment for children, people over 65 and people with kidney problems.

claims.evidence: NHS: if immune system is weakened (e.g. HIV/AIDS, bone marrow transplant) talk to your doctor about the best type of aciclovir.
claims.newSentence: For people with a weakened immune system, such as HIV or AIDS or a bone marrow transplant, the NHS advises talking to a doctor about the best type of aciclovir.

claims.evidence: First pass: 'sometimes tablets rather than cream' for weakened immune system; NHS retrieved text does not say this (emc says cold sore cream not recommended for immunocompromised patients, which is a different claim).
emc SmPC: probenecid and cimetidine increase aciclovir AUC / reduce renal clearance; aciclovir increases theophylline exposure.
claims.newSentence: UK product information says cimetidine and probenecid can raise aciclovir levels in the blood, and that aciclovir may raise theophylline levels.

claims.evidence: First pass named mycophenolate mofetil and aminophylline and said 'may not mix well with some tablets' as NHS wording; those two names were not seen in retrieved text.
First pass: no medicines are known to affect the cream or eye ointment. Not in retrieved text.
NHS: There's not enough information to say that herbal remedies or supplements are safe to take with aciclovir. They're not tested in the same way as pharmacy and prescription medicines.
claims.newSentence: The NHS says there is not enough information to show that herbal remedies or supplements are safe to take with aciclovir, and that they are not tested in the same way as pharmacy and prescription medicines.

claims.evidence: NHS common questions: yes, you can drink alcohol while taking aciclovir (its side-effects page adds do not drink too much).
claims.newSentence: The NHS says alcohol can be drunk while taking aciclovir.

claims.evidence: First pass: food and drink are not restricted. Not retrieved.
emc SmPC: aciclovir is eliminated mainly unchanged by the kidneys; dosage adjustment recommended in renal impairment.
claims.newSentence: Aciclovir is cleared through the kidneys, so the prescriber may adjust treatment for people with kidney problems.

claims.evidence: First pass: 'No routine monitoring is described on the NHS pages'. A claim about absence in pages not read in full; removed. Note: the monitoring gate field now rests on the kidney sentence only.
emc lists Zovirax Cold Sore Cream, Zovirax Cream, Zovirax 200 mg tablets and suspensions as UK aciclovir products.
claims.newSentence: brands UK Zovirax

claims.evidence: First pass: US brand Zovirax. No US source retrieved for brand.
NHS: you can buy aciclovir cold sore cream at most pharmacies and shops without a prescription.
claims.newSentence: The NHS says aciclovir cold sore cream can be bought at most pharmacies and shops without a prescription.

claims.evidence: Tablets, liquid and eye ointment being prescription-only in the UK is standard legal-status knowledge; the retrieved NHS text did not state it in so many words (NHS England pharmacy PGD for shingles aciclovir implies POM).
claims.newSentence: Prescription status for the other forms.

claims.evidence: NHS: forms listed; injections usually only in hospital.
claims.newSentence: The NHS describes tablets, a liquid to swallow, an eye ointment, a cold sore cream and a genital herpes cream; injections are usually given only in hospital.

claims.evidence: NHS: children can usually use the cream or ointment, and may be prescribed tablets for chickenpox and shingles.
claims.newSentence: Children can usually use the cream or ointment, and may be prescribed tablets for chickenpox and shingles.

claims.evidence: MedlinePlus topical acyclovir: does not cure cold sores or genital herpes, does not prevent outbreaks, does not stop the spread to other people.
claims.newSentence: MedlinePlus says acyclovir does not cure cold sores or genital herpes, does not prevent outbreaks of them and does not stop their spread to other people.

claims.evidence: NHS: if you or your partner have cold sores avoid kissing and oral sex until healed; reduces risk of passing on infection.
claims.newSentence: The NHS advises avoiding kissing and oral sex while a person or their partner has a cold sore, until the sores have healed, to reduce the risk of passing on the infection.

claims.evidence: Pharmacist advice sentence: general signposting; the NHS directs people to a pharmacist or doctor (see side effects page).
claims.newSentence: A pharmacist can advise whether it suits the infection in question.

notes: Doubts: (1) prescription status of non-cream forms is the single textbook sentence; (2) pregnancy: NHS page text was not retrieved beyond 'tell your doctor', so no reassurance is given; (3) the NHS pregnancy sub-page (pregnancy-breastfeeding-and-fertility-while-taking-or-using-aciclovir) came up but its content was not shown, worth a human glance; (4) alcohol: NHS side-effects page reportedly adds 'do not drink too much'; (5) US brand dropped; (6) monitoring field rests on SmPC kidney clearance only; (7) MedlinePlus oral page a681045 not re-confirmed, topical page used instead; (8) the last claim is a signposting sentence, classified supported by the NHS pattern only loosely.
